extracted.intended_audience: CHI 2024 reviewers, associate chairs, and program committee members (people assessing CHI paper submissions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reviewers assessing CHI 2024 paper submissions, including how to judge contribution, length, prior-publication, replication, confidentiality, and review quality. Targets the review process and reviewer responsibilities for conference decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary criterion — contribution to HCI
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this submission provide a strong contribution to the field of HCI? In all cases, a CHI paper must make an original research contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many ways a paper can make a contribution to HCI; review the paper appropriately for its contribution type (see 'Selecting a Subcommittee' and 'Guide to a Successful Submission' for types and associated criteria). Evaluate originality and strength of contribution as the primary basis for decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall recommendation must match written appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers decide the overall recommendation (Accept with minor revisions, Revise and Resubmit, and Reject) on each submission with written appraisal that matches with their recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a written appraisal that justifies the chosen recommendation. Short positive/negative reviews without justification are insufficient, especially if there are well-argued counter-reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review quality and expected length
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality review is typically about a page of written text; very short reviews are frustrating for authors, tend to be less constructive, and hurt the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always put yourself in the author's position: provide the level of detailed feedback you would want. Write detailed reviews whether or not you like the paper. Include constructive critique and actionable suggestions. Avoid extremely short reviews and unsupported assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibility for accuracy (including references and AI outputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer, you are responsible for the content and accuracy of your reviews, including the references cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using AI/LLM tools, ensure the outputs are accurate and relevant — LLMs are prone to plausible-sounding garbage. Do not rely on generated content without verification. Incorrect references or claims in a review reflect on the reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and handling unpublished content
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining confidentiality is crucial in the review process; quoting or disclosing papers under review must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying and pasting content from a manuscript into an online LLM may pose confidentiality risks. Reviewers should avoid sharing unpublished-paper content with any online tools that may store or process data in ways that could compromise confidentiality. Follow program and institutional confidentiality norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI/LLM tools for review-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online tools for editing and proofreading reviews is not prohibited but must be used with care; LLM-based tools prioritize prompt completion over accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accuracy and relevance of any AI-assisted suggestions. Avoid sharing manuscript text with tools that may store/process it. Take responsibility for all content produced or included in your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper length must be commensurate with contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper length should be commensurate with their contribution. There is no arbitrary maximum/minimum, but clarity and conciseness are vital. Discussion of length focuses on main text (not references, figures, tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must identify their paper as short (<5,000 words), long (typically 7,000–8,000 words), or excessively long (>12,000 words). Reviewers should judge whether length fits the contribution: reject papers whose lengths are incommensurate. Papers may be too long if repetitive/verbose; too short if they omit important details, neglect prior work, or tamper with formatting to save page count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short paper expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Short papers (less than 5,000 words) should present brief and focused research contributions that are noteworthy but may not be as comprehensive as long papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should not ask for more than appropriate for a short contribution; focus on what is needed for that short contribution rather than demanding the depth expected of a long paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessively long papers and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that far exceed typical lengths (>12,000 words) must justify why a shorter contribution is not suitable or possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of excessively long papers are required to justify the length to reviewers. Reviewers should weigh whether that justification is convincing. Excessively long submissions will receive additional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication / significant revision threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Material previously published in widely disseminated archival publications should not be republished unless the work has been significantly revised (roughly >25% new content) and significantly amplifies or clarifies the original material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of 'significance' is subjective and left to reviewers/committee members; consult ACM policies (ACM Policy on Pre-Publication Evaluation; ACM Policy on Prior Publication and Simultaneous Submissions). Work presented in a language other than English may be translated and published at CHI with the original author typically included and noted in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for non-archival venues and independent later work
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-archival venues (workshop presentations, posters, CHI Late-Breaking Work) do not count as prior publications. Work that overlaps with independently developed material published after the CHI submission (during review period) should not count against authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize authors for independent concurrent work that they could not have known about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication papers — sufficiency and reward for reproducibility materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive replication can be a significant contribution to HCI; replication papers are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitted replication work must include sufficient information for future replications. Efforts to include complete, well-organized supplementary materials (software, analysis code, data) that facilitate replication should be rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcommittee fit should not determine quality judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not judge the paper by how well it fits the subcommittee theme(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcommittee organization exists to improve reviewer matching; many papers will not cleanly fit. Evaluate papers on their own quality and contribution; any topic is valid if it fits the interests of a reasonable fraction of the overall CHI audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency in the way research results are reported can be a ground to doubt the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the 'Transparency' section in the Guide to a Successful Submission for discussion of transparency expectations across contribution types. Expect clear reporting of methods, data, analysis choices, and limitations.
